title: Smallest Park

jokes.text: Tom asks if Leslie just wants him to choose a new font, and Leslie confirms: 'Yes, essentially, I'd like you to choose a new font.' Then immediately makes Jerry 'number two guy on the new font project.'
jokes.setup: Leslie frames the assignment in grandiose terms: 'redesign our Parks Department logo,' 'make something amazing'
jokes.punchline: Tom deflates it — it's just choosing a font — and Leslie confirms this with complete sincerity, then immediately creates a bureaucratic hierarchy for this trivial task.
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks deflation joke — Leslie's earnest overselling punctured by Tom's blunt realism. The second beat (immediately hierarchizing the micro-project) layers the joke perfectly. Strong character integration: Leslie's bureaucratic sincerity and Tom's ego are both on display simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So you want me to redesign the entire Parks Department logo and visual brand?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! A complete overhaul. New colors, new fonts, new everything. Make it modern, make it pop!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so... what exactly are we talking about here? Like, how different?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, essentially just choose a new font.

jokes.text: Leslie defends putting Jerry as number three: 'He has been in this department a long time. I think maybe you could learn something from him.'
jokes.setup: Jerry has just been demoted to a nonsensical position.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense of Jerry is itself a form of condescension — implying the most he offers is tenure-based wisdom, not actual competence.
jokes.explanation: A good button on the Jerry joke — the defense is more insulting than no defense. Character-consistent but less structurally sharp than the preceding beats.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, you're number three on the font project.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: But Leslie, there are only two people total.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals her park is on a patch of former telephone booth concrete and is competing to be Indiana's smallest park, currently held by 'Martin Luther King, Junior, Park in Terryville. But guess what, Terryville sucks old car tires and so does Martin Luther...'
jokes.setup: Leslie is excitedly pitching the Smallest Park in Indiana concept.
jokes.punchline: Her competitive drive escalates so quickly she's about to slander Martin Luther King Jr. before catching herself.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. Leslie's competitive mania overrides her deeply held civic values so rapidly that she almost defames a civil rights icon over a micro-park. The interrupted sentence, the escalation, the absurdity of the stakes, and Leslie's immediate self-awareness are all perfectly constructed. This could only be Leslie Knope — she loves parks AND heroes, and the collision of those two things creates the joke. Highly quotable and earns its impact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've created an amazing, awe-inspiring park. It's 0.000003 square miles.

jokes.text: Leslie snaps back: 'No. He does not suck old car tires. He was one of the greatest men in history.' Then: 'I'm sorry. Sometimes, I get competitive.'
jokes.setup: Leslie nearly slanders MLK Jr. in a competitive parks tangent.
jokes.punchline: Her mortified self-correction is followed by the massive understatement 'Sometimes, I get competitive.'
jokes.explanation: A strong callback payoff. The correction is sincere and earnest (very Leslie), and the understatement 'Sometimes I get competitive' is the perfect button. Character integration is excellent — only Leslie would have this exact crisis of conscience at this exact speed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to break Terryville's park record. I don't care if I have to work twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. I will not rest until this park is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you need to sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Sleep is for people without vision, Ben. Sleep is for quitters and... and... people who aren't as driven as Martin Luther King Jr.— I mean, people who DON'T have dreams. Like MLK. He had dreams. Good dreams.

jokes.text: Ben and colleague are impressed by college course catalog 'shopping period'
jokes.setup: Andy marvels at the concept of sampling college classes freely.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, I did not graduate college because I did not attend it.' Delivered with cheerful earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The tautological self-explanation ('I did not graduate because I did not attend') is very Andy — cheerful, self-unaware, delivered as if it's a perfectly reasonable explanation. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I went to college for two and a half years. I got pretty close.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I would've graduated, but I ran out of money. Then I transferred to another school, but I ran out of money there too. Then I got really sick one semester, so I dropped out.

jokes.text: Andy explains why he didn't graduate college: 'I did not graduate college because I did not attend it.'
jokes.setup: The group discusses a 'crash course' at the local college.
jokes.punchline: Andy's confession that he simply never attended college is delivered with total matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. The tautological construction ('I did not graduate because I did not attend') is funny in its logical completeness — Andy explains everything while explaining nothing. Very character-specific: Andy's earnest self-awareness about his own obliviousness is a core trait.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: April's advice on college: 'Horizons are dumb. Never broaden your horizons. Just take something you're great at and get an easy A.'
jokes.setup: Ron advises Andy to broaden his horizons by exploring a new subject.
jokes.punchline: April flatly contradicts conventional wisdom with nihilistic pragmatism.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in April's voice — her deadpan anti-establishment cynicism delivered as life coaching. 'Horizons are dumb' is a quotable line. The irony that she's giving sincerely bad advice in complete sincerity is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've always said, if you want something, you have to work for it. Even education.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's why I'm not actively rooting against you, Andy.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional: 'Of all my coworkers, he is one of a small number whom I do not actively root against.'
jokes.setup: Ron says he values a good education and doesn't want Andy to waste his time.
jokes.punchline: His 'praise' of Andy is filtered through layers of Swanson-style damning with faint praise: not actively rooting against someone is the ceiling of his affection.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The construction is flawless — 'one of a small number whom I do not actively root against' is a masterclass in Ron Swanson's vernacular. The negation-within-negation (not rooting against = highest compliment) is the joke, and it could not be said by any other character. Extremely quotable, economical, and fully earned through character. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I care about Andy. There, I said it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm getting sappy.

jokes.text: Ron, immediately after his praise of Andy, says in confessional: 'There I go, getting all sappy.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered his version of a warm endorsement of Andy.
jokes.punchline: He self-critiques his comment as 'sappy,' underscoring how far his emotional register is from normal human warmth.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on Joke 8. The callback is instant and the self-awareness of the line makes it land harder. 'There I go, getting all sappy' as a response to 'I don't actively root against him' is the joke — the gap between what Ron thinks is sentimental and what actual sentimentality looks like. Excellent economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We need to pick a font for the new Parks logo. What do you think, Jerry?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I think we should go with something clean and modern. Maybe Helvetica?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I only like fonts that look like they could kill me.

jokes.text: Leslie opens a drawer at Ben's office expecting scissors and finds: 'Those are my pens and pencils.'
jokes.setup: Leslie declares she needs to 'ascertain the whereabouts of some oversized ceremonial scissors' and begins rifling through Ben's office.
jokes.punchline: She opens the wrong drawer and Ben corrects her — implying she was rummaging through his personal belongings with no hesitation.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/physical beat that illustrates Leslie's steamroller personality without commentary. Functional humor — the joke is entirely in the behavior, not the line. Works better visually than on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm like Steve Harvey. I got the mustache, I got the charm, I got the gravitas.

jokes.text: Tom on fonts: 'Okay. Now, see, I think that Comic Sans always screams fun. Right? But, man, those R's in Helvetica, they're just, you know like, really popping for me.'
jokes.setup: Tom is supposed to be doing a small, boring font assignment.
jokes.punchline: Tom is genuinely passionate and opinionated about fonts in the most Tom Haverford way — aesthetic swagger applied to a completely trivial subject.
jokes.explanation: Tom's aesthetic pretension applied to fonts is funny because it's so perfectly him — he treats every aesthetic decision as life-or-death. 'Those R's are really popping for me' is a good line. Solid character comedy, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm just learning the gor-tar. Still pretty new to it, you know?

jokes.text: Jerry responds to the font debate: 'I've never been more bored in my entire life. Who cares about letters? The only good font is the Sopranos one, where the R is a pistol.'
jokes.setup: Tom is passionately debating Comic Sans vs. Helvetica.
jokes.punchline: Jerry — normally the butt of jokes — delivers a brutally honest and objectively funny take: the only good font is a pop culture gun pun.
jokes.explanation: Jerry getting a rare good line is itself funny (subverted expectation), and the Sopranos font observation is a genuinely sharp, specific cultural reference that earns its laugh. 'Who cares about letters' is also a great button opener. The specificity ('where the R is a pistol') makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I have a confession to make. I've been pretending this whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm actually really good at guitar.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been playing since I was a kid.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We know.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? How?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, you've been playing 'Wonderwall' perfectly for the last twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Tom escalates the font project into a full department makeover: 'New uniforms, new signage, new color scheme. A whole new, sexy vibe.'
jokes.setup: Tom was asked to choose a font.
jokes.punchline: He's now pitching a total rebrand with 'sexy vibe' as his deliverable.
jokes.explanation: A solid Tom Haverford escalation moment — his ambition always overshoots the assignment. Functional character comedy but the 'sexy vibe' tag is the only truly sharp element.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You have the slenderest fingers I've ever seen. It's like you don't have any bones in them. They're like beautiful, beautiful worms.

jokes.text: Tom's confessional: 'Yes. Technically, my new job is my old job. But I'm not some boring Jerry Gergich-type guy. I'm more of a Steve Harvey. I dream big, I shake things up, and I always wear dope suits.'
jokes.setup: Tom is rationalizing his return to the Parks Department.
jokes.punchline: He positions himself as the Steve Harvey of local government — which is both completely delusional and oddly specific.
jokes.explanation: A great Tom Haverford confessional. 'Steve Harvey' as a self-identification benchmark is hilarious — specific, weird, and yet somehow accurate to Tom's self-image. The three-part structure (dream big, shake things up, dope suits) is well-constructed. Highly quotable. Only Tom could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to schedule the park opening so far in the future that by the time it actually opens, I'll have already accomplished all my other goals and won't care about this one anymore.

jokes.text: Andy shows off guitar knowledge in a beginner's class (naming frets, capos, explaining key changes), prompting the teacher to suggest the advanced class. Andy responds: 'Yeah, maybe I should. Dude, dumb it down. But I couldn't possibly, because I'm just a beginner. I barely haven't even ever seen a gor-tar.'
jokes.setup: Ron has advised Andy to take something he's great at and get an easy A. Andy picked Guitar for Beginners.
jokes.punchline: Andy demonstrates genuine expertise, gets called on it, and then deliberately mispronounces 'guitar' as 'gor-tar' to maintain his cover.
jokes.explanation: An excellent multi-layered joke. The irony of a seasoned musician trying to play dumb, the perfectly awkward cover ('I barely haven't even ever seen a gor-tar'), and the double negative grammar all work together. 'Gor-tar' is a fantastic comic invention — specific, quotable, and completely Andy. This is Andy Dwyer at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The park is too small for a basketball court. I mean, you'd literally just have a basketball rolling around in a parking lot.

jokes.text: Andy dramatically announces to the guitar class: 'Goodbye, everybody. Guess what. I was secretly an undercover rock star this whole time.'
jokes.setup: Andy is bored and leaving the guitar class.
jokes.punchline: His exit speech treats his cover identity as a spy mission — 'undercover rock star' — with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: A great exit line. 'I was secretly an undercover rock star this whole time' is the perfect Andy Dwyer declaration — grandiose, sincere, self-dramatizing, and completely unnecessary. The callback to his earlier deception gives it an extra layer. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: We won't be using actual lasers in this class.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No actual lasers? This is the worst day of my life.

jokes.text: Ron compliments a female student as they leave: 'For what it's worth, I think you would make an incredible brunette.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Andy are exiting the guitar class.
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers what he believes is a charming compliment — but it's a completely bizarre and borderline-offensive observation delivered with total Ron Swanson confidence.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson attempting to flirt is always gold. The specificity of the compliment ('incredible brunette') is perfectly wrong — it's not hostile, not sexual, just deeply strange in the way that only Ron Swanson compliments are. Excellent economy: one line, complete character portrait.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to redesign the Parks Department from the ground up. We need to be sleek, efficient, and profitable. Think of it like this: right now, we're a Pontiac Aztek. Ugly, nobody wants it, and it smells like desperation and broken dreams.

jokes.text: Leslie, in full crisis mode, hatches a plan to drag out the tiny park project: 'I should just drag out that tiny park project for as long as possible so Ben and I can keep working together.'
jokes.setup: Ann implies Leslie should let Ben go gracefully.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's takeaway is the complete opposite of what Ann meant — she devises an elaborate scheme to delay a 3-square-foot park.
jokes.explanation: Strong Leslie character comedy — her romantic feelings overriding her professional judgment is a core tension of the season, and the absurdity of scheming to delay the world's smallest park is perfectly calibrated. Ann's 'That's almost exactly the opposite of what I meant' is a great straight-man line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, that's it? We're done? But we haven't even gone through the zoning variance requests, or the noise ordinance amendments, or... anyone? Does anyone have any concerns? Complaints? Anything?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No? Really? This is so frustrating. I need you people to complain more. How am I supposed to solve problems if nobody tells me what the problems are?

jokes.text: Leslie announces a plan to get the neighborhood riled up to demand an Environmental Impact Report and keep working with Ben for 'at least another year.' Ann protests; Leslie: 'Good idea, Ann.' / 'No, Ann.' / 'Will you just shut your beautiful pie hole?'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to talk Leslie out of her scheme.
jokes.punchline: Leslie keeps 'hearing' Ann's objections as agreement, culminating in asking Ann to 'shut your beautiful pie hole' and stare at her silently in support.
jokes.explanation: The 'shut your beautiful pie hole' line is a genuine standout — it combines a silencing insult with a genuine compliment, which is very Leslie. The steamroller pattern of Leslie hearing only what she wants is well-executed here. 'Your quiet support means the world to me, as well as your tacit endorsement of all my behaviors' is also excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why would I take a Civil War class? I already know how it ends. The North wins.

jokes.text: Leslie announces the grand opening of 'Pawnee's smallest park on November 12th, 2070.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining how she'll delay the tiny park project indefinitely to keep working with Ben.
jokes.punchline: She gives a specific date 58 years in the future as the 'grand opening' — with complete deadpan sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '2070' is key — a vague 'far future' would be less funny. Leslie making it an official announcement date sells the delusion. Good absurdist button on the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: Joan of Arc showed incredible courage facing execution, knowing she was right.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That sounds amazing. Do you think they'd let me do that?

jokes.text: Leslie tries to delay the public meeting's first question: 'Oh, wait. Whoa, whoa, whoa. Where's the fire? Let's get to know each other first. Tell me about your childhood.'
jokes.setup: A community member raises a hand immediately at the public meeting for the park.
jokes.punchline: Leslie stalls with an entirely inappropriate personal intimacy request — asking about the citizen's childhood at a government meeting.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Leslie using government meetings to establish personal rapport is very her. 'Tell me about your childhood' at a parks public forum is the right level of absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Women's Studies? That sounds amazing!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It is. It's a real class.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Women's... Studies... Women's Lasers!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, Studies.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's what I said. Women's Lasers.

jokes.text: Community member Rose: 'Basketball courts attract undesirables to my community... because there is a definite type of person I associate with basketball, and I'd rather not have that type of person nearby.' Ben and Leslie race to stop her before she says something racist.
jokes.setup: A community member asks if there will be a basketball court.
jokes.punchline: She keeps telegraphing a racist statement while Ben and Leslie desperately interrupt her — the comedy is in how long the near-miss is extended.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed cringe sequence. The escalating panic of Ben and Leslie, and the show's deft handling of implied racism without having the character actually say it, is skilled writing. The interruptions become increasingly frantic. Strong impact from audience discomfort-turned-relief.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm taking Women's Studies.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: To learn about women and their studies.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not... never mind.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Did you know that women invented the laser? No wait, that was lasers. Women invented... the study of lasers?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Get out of my office.

jokes.text: Leslie pivots Rose's near-racist comment into a spontaneous forum on prejudice: 'You bring up a very good point. Intolerance. Can we be doing more? I'd like to hear from each and every one of you about a time when prejudice has touched your lives.'
jokes.setup: Rose is about to say something racist about basketball courts.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's pivot is so fast and so politically earnest that she turns a near-catastrophe into a diversity seminar — a completely unhinged but very Leslie solution.
jokes.explanation: Leslie converting a government meeting into an impromptu prejudice forum is a perfect expression of her character: solve every crisis with enthusiasm and civic engagement, even inappropriate ones. Strong character integration and a clever structural pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: Wait, you work for the government?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I do, but I'm also a whistleblower exposing a massive government conspiracy.

jokes.text: Andy in laser class: 'Where are the lasers?' followed by Ron: 'He's not even using a laser pointer.'
jokes.setup: The professor explains that 'Introduction to Lasers' is a theory class about the electromagnetic spectrum.
jokes.punchline: Andy's disappointment is immediate and specific; Ron validates it by noting the professor isn't even using a laser pointer.
jokes.explanation: A great double act. Andy's childlike expectation (actual lasers to play with) and Ron's supporting observation (the professor doesn't even use a laser pointer) work together perfectly. Ron validating Andy's complaint rather than correcting it is a great character choice — Ron respects direct experience over abstraction.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, we really just need you to pick a simple font for the document.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Simple? SIMPLE?! I am not a simple man, Jerry. I am a complex tapestry of ambition, style, and unbridled charisma. My font choices are a reflection of my soul. I will not be confined to your pedestrian notions of simplicity.

jokes.text: Andy asks the laser professor: 'Curious. When will you be bringing out the lasers for me to play with? And will we start with the small lasers or could we go just straight to the big lasers, in terms of playing with them?'
jokes.setup: The professor has established this is a theory class with no actual lasers.
jokes.punchline: Andy asks about laser logistics in total earnestness, including the size progression of lasers he expects to play with.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'where are the lasers' to a detailed logistical inquiry about laser size progression ('small lasers... straight to the big lasers, in terms of playing with them') is very well constructed. The phrase 'in terms of playing with them' is the perfect Andy Dwyer verbal tic. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie steamrolls me in our partnership. I tried to tell her we shouldn't work together, but she just kept talking over me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So I made a public declaration about it.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional after learning the laser class has no actual lasers: 'One of the most significant bummers of my lifetime.'
jokes.setup: The professor confirms they will not be using actual lasers.
jokes.punchline: Andy, in confessional, delivers a formal superlative assessment: this is one of his life's most significant disappointments.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy. The formal register ('most significant bummers of my lifetime') applied to Andy's childlike disappointment about not playing with lasers is the joke. 'Bummers' is the perfect word — informal but the most severe word Andy has. Very quotable, very rewatchable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey ladies, I'm here to register for Women's Studies. I'm Andy Dwyer, and I'm a feminist.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: That's great. Have you taken any prerequisite courses?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, but I've watched a lot of Lifetime movies, and I'm pretty sure I know what's going on.

jokes.text: Tom's rebranding pitch presents the 'new community center' that 'looks like an Apple Store.' Tom: 'Today I'm a Beverly Hills plastic surgeon. And the Parks Department is a wrinkly old housewife in her early 30s. I'm about to work a miracle.'
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching his expanded vision for the department.
jokes.punchline: The plastic surgeon/wrinkly housewife metaphor is both unexpected and very Tom — glamorous, vaguely offensive, and entirely self-aggrandizing.
jokes.explanation: The metaphor is Tom Haverford at his most vivid — not just saying the Parks Department needs updating but casting himself as a celebrity plastic surgeon doing it. 'A wrinkly old housewife in her early 30s' is the gem here: the specific, contradictory ageism is very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'd like to register for Women's Studies, please.

dialogue.speaker: Registrar
dialogue.line: That class is full.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh man. Do you know when the next Women's Studies is? I've been trying to catch Women for like three months.

jokes.text: Leslie tries to keep the meeting going by drawing out a silent community member: 'This gentleman wants to say something.' Man: 'No, I don't.' Leslie's colleague: 'Come on, Mel. You're always up in arms about something.' Mel: 'No, I'm not. I'm not always up in arms about something.' Leslie: 'That's the spirit! Talk to me about what's bothering you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs the meeting to last longer to delay the park.
jokes.punchline: She tries to manufacture outrage by pressuring a reluctant man, misreading his protests as engagement.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. Leslie misinterpreting 'No, I'm not always up in arms' as enthusiasm is a nice irony. 'That's the spirit!' as a response to denial is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I can't take April's parents' money. That's not who I am.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna start a street begging business. I'll be like a regular beggar, but with better jokes.

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: 'I once hosted a forum about a new bike rack that lasted seven hours. Now, when I need these people to complain, they're done in 45 minutes?'
jokes.setup: The community meeting wraps up faster than Leslie wanted.
jokes.punchline: Leslie is frustrated that the notoriously complaint-prone Pawnee citizens aren't complaining enough when she needs them to.
jokes.explanation: An excellent irony: the person who usually suffers from Pawnee's relentless civic complaints is now frustrated they're being too cooperative. 'A bike rack that lasted seven hours' is a perfect worldbuilding detail that makes Pawnee feel real and funny. The reversal is well-structured and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're a steamroller.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? A steamroller?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes. You just steamroll over people and their feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I do not steamroll people!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're like a steamroller that's lost its brakes, barreling down a hill, crushing everything in its path, and you don't even notice because you're too busy planning the next thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That is not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're a steamroller that's on fire, Leslie. A flaming steamroller with a megaphone, screaming about your vision, and anyone who disagrees gets flattened and set ablaze.

jokes.text: Ron, looking at the college course catalog: 'Check it out. You can get credit for playing intramural Frisbee Golf.' Andy: 'You can take a class on the Civil War.' Ron: 'Why would I take a class on something that's already happened?'
jokes.setup: Ron and Andy are browsing college courses.
jokes.punchline: Ron's anti-intellectualism takes a bizarre form: he sees no point in studying historical events because they're over. It's logical within his worldview but completely insane.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron's rejection of Civil War history ('Why would I take a class on something that's already happened?') is perfectly constructed Ron Swanson logic — internally consistent but absurd from the outside. It reveals his worldview (practical, anti-academic, present-focused) in a single line. Extremely quotable. This is the Ron Swanson joke that would circulate as a GIF. High craft, fully earned.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're a steamroller, Leslie. You push too hard.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, a steamroller would be a more accurate description if I were flattening things, which I'm not. I'm more of a... a very efficient organizer who occasionally gets ahead of herself.

jokes.text: Andy in the Women's Studies class: 'I want to be burned at the stake.' Then later: 'I wholeheartedly agree. If that woman weren't so violently opposed to marriage, I think I would propose to her.'
jokes.setup: The Women's Studies professor lectures about Joan of Arc and institutional oppression of women.
jokes.punchline: Andy responds to the empowerment lecture with unqualified enthusiasm and a marriage proposal impulse — missing the irony entirely.
jokes.explanation: Andy's enthusiasm for Women's Studies is great character comedy — he has no irony filter, so he takes all of it at face value and loves it. 'If that woman weren't so violently opposed to marriage, I think I would propose to her' is a beautifully constructed contradiction: he's fallen for a radical feminist while missing that she would reject him for existing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm like a steamroller, just flattening everything in my path, and I'm not going to stop until... until the... the roller thing... what do you call that?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The roller?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, thank you.

jokes.text: 'Andy Dwyer will be taking Women's Lasers.' Ron: 'Women's Studies.' Andy: 'Sorry. God, I cannot stop thinking about lasers. Women's Studies. Is there such a thing as Women's Lasers? That would be my number one pick.'
jokes.setup: Andy has chosen Women's Studies as his class.
jokes.punchline: Andy accidentally says 'Women's Lasers,' combining his two obsessions, and then sincerely advocates for Women's Lasers as a course that should exist.
jokes.explanation: A perfect synthesis of the episode's two Andy threads (lasers + Women's Studies) into one absurdist portmanteau: 'Women's Lasers.' The running gag pays off here with maximum efficiency. 'That would be my number one pick' elevates it — Andy's not confused, he genuinely wishes this subject existed. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I've been doing everything the same way for over 30 years.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Same clothes, same routines, same ID card photo.

jokes.text: The riled-up community member Joe confronts Leslie: 'Don't you work for the government?' Leslie: 'I do, Joe. Yeah, that's how I know just how high this conspiracy goes.'
jokes.setup: Joe is suspicious about the park and demands to know why there was no Environmental Impact Report.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, who IS the government, confirms the conspiracy — validating the paranoid citizen's fears by essentially agreeing the government is conspiring.
jokes.explanation: Excellent irony: the government employee confirming that 'this conspiracy goes very high' because she IS the conspiracy. The citizen's logic ('don't you work for the government?') is completely sound, which makes Leslie's response funnier. Very quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, I need help paying for college.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to create a scholarship in my name. The Ron Swanson Memorial Scholarship for Excellence in Woodworking and Breakfast Foods.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, you're not dead.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: Tom's 'Ranger Reality Show' pitch: shows current park rangers and says 'What are they up to? No one cares. They're boring and I hate them. But coming this spring to the Style Network, Ranger Reality Show.'
jokes.setup: Tom is continuing to pitch increasingly off-task department ideas.
jokes.punchline: Tom dismisses actual park rangers as boring and hates them, then pivots to a reality show pitch — specifically for the Style Network.
jokes.explanation: Tom's contempt for real government work and his instinct to turn everything into entertainment is well-expressed here. 'I hate them' as bureaucratic assessment is funny. The Style Network specificity is good. Solid but not exceptional Tom content.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm helping Andy because I believe in investing in people who show promise. It's practical, it's efficient, and frankly, I have more money than I could spend in ten lifetimes anyway. I've got at least three barrels of it buried in various locations around Pawnee.

jokes.text: Leslie tries to extend the protest meeting by stopping a man from leaving for the bathroom: 'Hey. Where are you going, Joe? Bathroom break? No. Get back over there. I'll find you a bottle or something.'
jokes.setup: The meeting is wrapping up faster than Leslie wanted.
jokes.punchline: Leslie offers to find a bottle for a man to urinate into rather than lose a meeting attendee — fully committed to her scheme.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'don't leave' to 'I'll find you a bottle' is a great comedic jump. Leslie's shamelessness in service of her goal is perfectly portrayed. The specificity of 'a bottle or something' (the 'or something' makes it worse) is great.

jokes.text: Chris repeatedly shouts 'Dream Team!' despite Ben explaining the partnership is dysfunctional. Chris: 'Dream Team!' Ben: 'Yeah. But we're not.' Chris: 'Dream Team!'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to explain to Chris that he and Leslie don't work well as a team.
jokes.punchline: Chris keeps shouting 'Dream Team!' as if the phrase itself will fix the problem — he is constitutionally incapable of processing negative information.
jokes.explanation: Chris's relentless positivity is a core character trait and 'Dream Team!' used as a verbal override of valid complaints is well-executed. The repetition structure works. Ben having to explain the dysfunction to someone who refuses to hear it creates good cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thank you, thank you. I'm glad you all appreciate my vision.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, this is incredible. You've really outdone yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know. I'm basically a design genius at this point.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Actually, I came up with that logo back in 1987.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Nobody asked you, Jerry. You're number four now.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I was number three yesterday.

jokes.text: Chris, after being told the Dream Team is dead: 'Wow. That was very hard to hear. So many negative words. I just need to process this.'
jokes.setup: Ben has definitively told Chris he doesn't want to work with Leslie anymore.
jokes.punchline: Chris, the hyper-positive optimist, is visibly shaken by negative words — and needs recovery time as if from physical trauma.
jokes.explanation: 'So many negative words' is a good line — Chris quantifying negativity as an assault. Well within Chris's character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I respect that. You don't want to work together anymore. I get it. So... do you want to go out sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Come on, Ben. We have great chemistry. We make each other laugh.

jokes.text: Chris dismisses the 'Dream Team' breakup: 'Okay, the Dream Team is dead. But you guys had a great run. Oh, and the park is open. Yay. Ha-ha! Good job with that.'
jokes.setup: Chris has processed the Dream Team dissolution.
jokes.punchline: His recovery is instant — he moves on with a cheerful 'yay' and a laugh, treating a serious interpersonal moment as a minor inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Good Chris button. The snap recovery after 'processing' is funny. 'Oh, and the park is open. Yay' is a nice throwaway that puts the whole episode's central project in comic perspective — it was always going to be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I have no idea what you're talking about. I'm just gonna go back to my desk and eat a tub of ice cream.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: Mr. Dwyer, that's not even close to the correct answer.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know. But you know what? That's cool. Ice cream's delicious.

jokes.text: Andy greets the Women's Studies registration desk: 'Hello, ma'am, who is just as equal as men. I would like one ticket for Women.'
jokes.setup: Andy is enthusiastically signing up for Women's Studies.
jokes.punchline: His feminist greeting is sincere but completely wrong — 'one ticket for Women' treats the class like a theme park attraction.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'One ticket for Women' is brilliant — Andy's sincerity is total, his feminism is wholehearted, and his execution is entirely wrong. The greeting ('just as equal as men') is also perfect: he's trying to use the right vocabulary but the construction is garbled. This is extremely quotable and the character integration is nearly perfect. Andy Dwyer as accidental absurdist.

jokes.text: Andy's plan to pay for Women's Studies: 'I'm going to beg for money on the street like a drug addict.' April: 'No.' Andy: 'Yep.'
jokes.setup: The Women's Studies class costs $940.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate solution is street begging (specifically 'like a drug addict'), delivered as a sober plan.
jokes.explanation: The specificity 'like a drug addict' is the joke — not just begging but Andy identifying the reference class. April's flat 'No' / Andy's firm 'Yep' is a good beat. Character-specific: Andy's solutions are always drastic.

jokes.text: April's reaction to the $940 class cost: 'Oh, my God. Everything in my life is going wrong right now. Whose fault is this? I demand to know.'
jokes.setup: The class costs $940, which April didn't know.
jokes.punchline: April immediately catastrophizes and demands accountability for a situation she partially caused, in her deadpan dramatic style.
jokes.explanation: April's dramatic victimhood ('everything in my life is going wrong') over tuition she didn't expect to pay is well-characterized. 'I demand to know' is a good button. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Ann confronts Leslie about being a steamroller: 'You made me watch all eight Harry Potter movies. I don't even like Harry Potter.' Leslie: 'That's insane. You love Harry Potter. You've seen all eight movies.'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to explain Leslie's steamroller tendencies with specific examples.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately contradicts Ann's stated experience of her own preferences — demonstrating the steamroller behavior in real time while arguing about it.
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural highlight. Ann says 'I don't like Harry Potter' and Leslie immediately tells her 'you love Harry Potter, you've seen all eight movies' — which is EXACTLY the behavior Ann is describing. The joke is that Leslie steamrolls Ann ABOUT the steamrolling, in the same breath, without irony. This is the best kind of character comedy: the form IS the content. Exceptional structure, fully earned, and extremely quotable. One of the strongest jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Ann: 'When we go out to a bar, you order my drinks for me.' Leslie: 'Because you order white wine and it gives you a headache.' Ann: 'Well, it's my headache.'
jokes.setup: Ann is listing examples of Leslie's steamroller behavior.
jokes.punchline: 'Well, it's my headache' — Ann reclaims her right to suffer consequences of her own choices, a perfect encapsulation of autonomy vs. Leslie's paternalistic care.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant two-line exchange. Ann's 'it's my headache' is perfectly constructed — it's simultaneously funny and philosophically correct. Leslie's logic is impeccable (the wine gives you a headache) and Ann's response is unanswerable (yes, but it's my headache to have). The economy is exceptional. This is a quotable line that works as a principle.

jokes.text: Ann finally gets through to Leslie: 'You're a steamroller! You are a massive, enormous, runaway steamroller, with no brakes and a cement brick on the gas pedal.'
jokes.setup: Leslie keeps interrupting Ann's attempts to tell her she's a steamroller — ironically proving the point.
jokes.punchline: Ann finally gets to complete her metaphor, and the elaboration — 'no brakes and a cement brick on the gas pedal' — is the perfect comedic excess for what started as a simple metaphor.
jokes.explanation: The comedic structure is excellent: Leslie keeps interrupting Ann's attempts to call her a steamroller, which is itself steamrolling. When Ann finally gets through, the elaboration is disproportionately intense — 'no brakes and a cement brick on the gas pedal' has the energy of someone who has been waiting a long time to say this.

jokes.text: Leslie's self-critique: 'I'm the worst.' Ann corrects her: 'No, you're very passionate.' Leslie: 'Well, then, you should call me a bulldozer rather than a steamroller.'
jokes.setup: Leslie accepts she's a steamroller.
jokes.punchline: Her correction is that 'bulldozer' is the more accurate heavy machinery metaphor — splitting hairs about which earthmover best describes her personality.
jokes.explanation: A great character beat. Leslie accepting 'steamroller' as a label but then litigating which construction vehicle is more accurate is perfectly Leslie — she takes criticism, processes it through her own framework, and comes out with a technical correction. Very quotable and a strong button on the steamroller arc.

jokes.text: Leslie searches for the metaphor: 'Okay. Well, this steamroller is hanging up her...' [long pause] 'The roll-y thing on the front of the machine. What do you, what do you call that?' Ann: 'Roller?' Leslie: 'Probably. Okay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a metaphorical declaration about retiring her steamroller ways.
jokes.punchline: She can't complete the metaphor because she doesn't know the word for the steamroller's rolling mechanism — they settle on 'probably roller.'
jokes.explanation: The comic deflation of a sincere emotional moment by not knowing the word 'roller' is gentle and well-timed. 'The roll-y thing on the front of the machine' is endearing. Ann's 'Roller?' and Leslie's 'Probably. Okay.' is a great anticlimactic button. This works on rewatch because the sincerity of the moment makes the word-fail funnier.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Well, this steamroller is hanging up her... [pause] ...The roll-y thing on the front of the machine. What do you, what do you call that?' Ann: 'Roller?' Leslie: 'Probably. Okay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a dramatic declaration about being done steamrolling people.
jokes.punchline: Her inspirational metaphor collapses because she doesn't know the word for the thing she's hanging up — 'the roll-y thing on the front of the machine.'
jokes.explanation: A lovely deflation joke. The dramatic 'this steamroller is hanging up her...' pause creates anticipation for a rousing closing line, then completely stalls on 'the roll-y thing on the front of the machine.' The anti-climax is well-earned. Ann's tentative 'Roller?' and Leslie's resigned 'Probably. Okay' are perfect buttons.

jokes.text: Jerry comforts Tom with a 'triple-decker ham-and-cheese from the cafeteria. Always makes me feel better.' Tom: 'Two pathetic guys, eating pathetic sandwiches. Sounds terrific.'
jokes.setup: Tom is deflated about being told to stay in his lane on the rebranding project.
jokes.punchline: Tom accepts the sandwich but immediately reframes the situation as maximum sadness — the shared sandwich becomes a symbol of defeat.
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment. 'Two pathetic guys, eating pathetic sandwiches' has good rhythm but is fairly predictable. Tom calling the cafeteria sandwich pathetic while accepting it is mildly funny.

jokes.text: Jerry describes his life as a cautionary tale: 'I guess I'm Jerry now. After work, I'll just go home, straight to my boring house, kiss my wife, and have a home-cooked meal with my three beautiful daughters. What a miserable life.'
jokes.setup: Tom is wallowing and comparing himself to Jerry.
jokes.punchline: Tom lists Jerry's life — which is objectively wonderful — as if it's a tragedy. The joke is that Jerry has an enviable life that everyone in the office ignores.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most satisfying Jerry jokes — and Jerry's not even saying it. Tom describes 'the Jerry life' as rock bottom, but the elements (loving wife, home-cooked meals, beautiful daughters) are the best possible life outcome. The show has always used Jerry this way: he's actually living the dream while everyone condescends to him. 'What a miserable life' as a button is excellent.

jokes.text: Jerry reveals his original ID card from his first day on the job: 'Heck, I still use my original ID card from my first day on the job.' [Shows it to Tom; Tom has a stunned reaction and runs off.]
jokes.setup: Jerry explains his coping strategy for work: doing everything the same way every day.
jokes.punchline: His original ID card photo from 30+ years ago is apparently so extraordinary that Tom immediately abandons his sandwich and runs to use it for the vintage logo idea.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual/reaction beat. We don't see the card but Tom's response ('Oh my God. I've got to go.') tells us everything. The setup (Jerry's old-school consistency) pays off as an accidental creative goldmine. Good structural use of the visual gag.

jokes.text: Andy's fundraising scheme on display: 'Mouse Rat CD. $30. Candy bars. $50. $50. God, people here are so cheap.'
jokes.setup: Andy needs to raise $940 for Women's Studies.
jokes.punchline: Andy is selling candy bars for $50 each and is frustrated that people won't buy them — his pricing is the problem, not the concept.
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete inability to understand market pricing and blaming customers is very character-specific. '$50. $50.' followed by 'people here are so cheap' is a good construction.

jokes.text: April tells Ron she's back working at her old job. Andy: 'Do you want a shoe shine? It's $100.' April: 'Laugh all you want, Kyle. I already took the money out of your wallet.'
jokes.setup: They're fundraising desperately for tuition.
jokes.punchline: April has already pickpocketed Kyle while he was laughing at them — darkly competent in a way Andy is not.
jokes.explanation: April stealing from Kyle while he mocks them is dark, confident, and completely April. 'I already took the money out of your wallet' delivered deadpan is a great line. Her proactive crime vs. Andy's failed commerce is a good character contrast.

jokes.text: Ron announces a 'Ron Swanson Scholarship' and gives Andy money. Andy: 'I don't think so. I don't remember applying for that.'
jokes.setup: Andy needs money for Women's Studies.
jokes.punchline: Andy is suspicious of the scholarship because he doesn't remember applying — not catching that Ron made it up on the spot to help him.
jokes.explanation: Andy's skepticism about his own scholarship is a beautiful Andy Dwyer moment. His bureaucratic instinct (I'd remember applying) kicks in at the exact wrong time. And Ron's generosity filtered through made-up institutional branding is very Ron.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional explaining the scholarship: 'One thing I promised myself when I buried gold in my backyard was that I'd never be a hoarder or a miser about it.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just given Andy money for college.
jokes.punchline: His stated principle against being a hoarder is rooted in the fact that he literally buries gold in his backyard — which IS hoarding.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Ron Swanson line. The premise that he buries gold in his backyard is delivered as completely normal backstory. His principle against hoarding while burying literal gold is a perfect internal contradiction that Ron cannot see. 'I buried gold in my backyard' as casual biography is what makes this special. Could not be said by anyone but Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Ann's cheesecake admission: 'She once made me eat an entire cheesecake at a potluck so she didn't look bad.' Ben: 'You ate an entire cheesecake? Why didn't you just throw it away?' Ann: 'Because with everything she's done for me, I would eat 10 cheesecakes for her. Also, PS, it was delicious and amazing, like everything she does.'
jokes.setup: Ann is describing how difficult Leslie can be, using the cheesecake as an example.
jokes.punchline: She begins criticizing Leslie, then immediately pivots to declaring she'd eat 10 cheesecakes for her, and concludes with 'it was delicious and amazing, like everything she does' — an accidental declaration of love.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful Ann moment. She's supposed to be building a case against Leslie, but her loyalty overwhelms her argument in real time. The 'PS, it was delicious and amazing, like everything she does' pivot is the joke — she accidentally ends up praising Leslie to the person she's trying to convince. The structure mirrors the steamroller dynamic: Ann gets steamrolled by her own feelings about Leslie.

jokes.text: Tom's vintage logo pitch: Using the old 1970s logo as a limited edition on hats, posters, and T-shirts. Chris: 'It is possibly the best idea anyone has had in this government in 100 years.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been shooting for the moon all episode on an overblown rebranding scheme.
jokes.punchline: His actual good idea — simple, rooted in nostalgia, inspired by Jerry's old ID card — is praised as the best in 100 years of government. The over-the-top Chris reaction mirrors Tom's own grandiosity.
jokes.explanation: A decent payoff on Tom's arc — the good idea comes from accidentally listening to Jerry. Chris's hyperbolic praise is in character. Functional but not a standout joke.

jokes.text: Tom credits Jerry as 'my number four' for the vintage logo idea: 'He shared some words of wisdom with me today. And while he was yammering on about whatever, I happened to see his old ID card.'
jokes.setup: Tom is crediting the inspiration for his best idea to Jerry.
jokes.punchline: His 'credit' involves calling Jerry's wisdom 'yammering on about whatever' and making clear he only accidentally benefited from it.
jokes.explanation: Tom gives credit while simultaneously taking it away. 'While he was yammering on about whatever' is a great construction — it's a compliment and dismissal simultaneously. Good callback structure.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ben: 'I wasn't sure you were going to come.' Ben: 'Well, I got very curious when you only left me one voicemail message instead of your usual 20.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been trying to be less intense. Ben shows up.
jokes.punchline: Ben's curiosity was triggered by the anomaly of ONE voicemail — revealing that 20 is Leslie's normal operating volume.
jokes.explanation: A sharp character-revealing joke. Twenty voicemails as a baseline is a great number — specific enough to be funny, high enough to be alarming. Ben's concern triggered by the absence of volume is a well-structured character beat that reinforces both Leslie's intensity and Ben's affection despite it.

jokes.text: Leslie offers Ben a seat: 'Here, have a seat. But only if you want to.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is actively trying to not steamroll Ben.
jokes.punchline: Her version of not steamrolling — offering a seat with explicit opt-out — is both sincere and absurdly over-corrected.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective joke about Leslie's overcorrection. The 'but only if you want to' appended to a basic hospitality offer shows she's trying so hard not to steamroll that she's become comically deferential. Character integration is high.

jokes.text: Andy on his first day of Women's Studies: 'Oh, crap. I forgot my books and my computer.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks if Andy is ready for his first day. Andy says yes.
jokes.punchline: Immediately: 'Oh, crap. I forgot my books and my computer.' He was not ready.
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional character beat. The 'as ready as I'll ever be' → immediate failure is a predictable structure but it's executed cleanly and is true to Andy. Not a strong joke on its own but works as a grace note.

jokes.text: Women's Studies professor lecturing: 'We need to start teaching women football. Teaching women UFC. Teaching them to drive trucks without crashing.' [Student]: 'Hey. Maybe I'm only sexy, and maybe that's all you see. But at least you can give me extra money, tip money and stuff. I'll flirt with you, write my name on a napkin. They're going to do it in a right kind of legal way that empowers prostitution. We don't rest until we get that. That will be progress.'
jokes.setup: Andy and Ron are in a Women's Studies class with a passionate, chaotic professor.
jokes.punchline: The class descends into increasingly radical and incoherent positions, culminating in a student advocating for 'empowering prostitution' as the feminist endgame.
jokes.explanation: The weakest of the Women's Studies jokes. The characterization of the class as chaotic and extreme feels broad rather than specific, and the student's speech is difficult to parse clearly even in context. The humor relies on 'this class is crazy' which is less crafted than the earlier Andy reactions to the content. The structure is loose compared to the episode's better jokes.

jokes.text: Andy in Women's Studies, confidently answers a question wrong, then says: 'I thought... I thought maybe it was. When I was... I'll get them next time. Back to you, Professor.'
jokes.setup: Andy is sitting in Women's Studies and has presumably attempted to answer a question.
jokes.punchline: 'Back to you, Professor' — Andy treats the classroom like a news broadcast, surrendering the floor back to the professor as if he had voluntarily been on camera.
jokes.explanation: Excellent closer for Andy's college arc. 'Back to you, Professor' is a brilliantly specific phrase — it's Andy's social framework (news broadcasts) applied to a classroom. His gracious concession of the floor ('I'll get them next time') paired with the broadcast sign-off is very Andy. Highly quotable and a perfect button.

tmdb_overview: Leslie uses her new tourist attraction as a way to spend more time with Ben. Meanwhile, Ron and April encourage Andy to go to college, and Chris tasks Tom and Jerry with revamping the Parks and Rec logo.
insight: Ben's budget-cutting chaos escalates into 38 jokes—Parks' densest governmental absurdist episode.
